newsitem.title: KUWAIT: U.S. troops for Kuwait, Patriots deployed.
newsitem.headline: U.S. troops for Kuwait, Patriots deployed.

text.p: The U.S. Cavalry started heading off to Kuwait on Wednesday to deter what the Gulf state and ally Washington see as threats by Iraq, which is believed to still possess Scud missiles.
The first of the 3,500 U.S. ground troops left by plane for tiny, oil-rich Kuwait, where the United States on Tuesday deployed eight Patriot launchers.

A U.N. team in charge of scrapping Iraq's weapons of mass destruction says 16 of Baghdad's Scud missiles were unaccounted for. Western military sources say Iraq is believed to still have Scuds and a capability to develop chemical arms.

The four-barrelled-Patriot launchers join others and hundreds of the Scud-busting missiles that Kuwait bought from the United States after it led a coalition in 1991 to free the Gulf Arab state from a seven-month Iraqi occupation.
The additional Patriots and a 100-strong crew were moved to Kuwait earlier this week from another location in the Arabian Peninsula, U.S. officers said.
"We ask God to...make us victorious against our enemy," Kuwait's Crown Prince and Prime Minister Sheikh Saad al-Abdulla al-Sabah told the Supreme Planning Council on Wednesday.

"These developments emphasis a fact that should never abandon our minds, which is that the Iraqi regime did not give up its aggressive intentions and expansionist plans...," the Kuwait News Agency quoted him as saying.
"As long as this evil remained on our border we should not feel reassured or at ease," he added.

The U.S. deployment is part of a huge U.S. build-up in the region that includes sending eight Stealth bombers to Kuwait. Western sources said the hi-tech jets had started training and familiarisation flights but were not as yet flying over Iraq.
Kuwait said it expected the United States and possibly other Gulf Arab states to share the hefty deployment costs.
U.S. President Bill Clinton said on Tuesday he had ordered 3,500 1st Cavalry Division troops to Kuwait "to keep Saddam Hussein in a box".
U.S. officials said several hundred of the soldiers left Texas on Wednesday.
Washington earlier this month sent two Patriot batteries and U.S. soldiers to Saudi Arabia after Iraq fired missiles at U.S. warplanes last week in the latest U.S. standoff with Baghdad.
The row began late last month when Baghdad's forces intervened to help a Kurdish faction in northern Iraq -- an area closed to them since the end of the Gulf War.

Washington retaliated by firing 44 cruise missiles at air defence targets in southern Iraq. The U.N. said on Wednesday some of the missiles violated the Iraq-Kuwait demilitarised zone set up by the world body after the Gulf War.

Major-General Gian Santillo, Force Commander of the U.N. Iraq-Kuwait Observer Mission (UNIKOM), said two unidentified warplanes were seen on Wednesday circling over the 15 km-wide (10 miles) zone in breach of the terms of the DMZ.
UNIKOM observers saw "a number" of the cruise missiles.
"It was a violation," Santillo told Reuters. Like with the aircraft on Wednesday, it was noted by UNIKOM and passed on to the world body in New York.
Like some Western officers in the region, he said UNIKOM had not seen any suspicious Iraqi military activity close to the border in recent weeks, dismissing earlier unconfirmed reports.
Whatever the outcome of this latest crisis, Kuwaitis are glad to see Washington rushing to their aid.

"Why don't we create a strong link with the United States and make our relations with the American nation deeper, to the extent of a union, provided that we reserve our right of sovereignty," wrote Salah al-Sayer in al-Anba.
